I. INTRODUCTION AND FACTS
Defendants, Mark E. Houser and Charlene Houser, are and were at all times relevant the owners of the property located at 273 Cranz Place, Akron, Ohio. Plaintiff Teri Carroll was a guest of the Housers' tenant, Patrick Morrison. (See Rental Agreement attached to Defendant's Motion for Summary Judgment as "Exhibit A"). The Housers initiated eviction proceedings against Mr. Morrison, Plaintiff Terri Carroll and all other occupants on December 11, 2005 for failure to pay rent as required by the lease agreement. (See Notice To Leave The Premises attached to Defendant's Motion for Summary Judgment as "Exhibit C"). Twelve days later, on December 23, 2005, Plaintiff left the house, walking down the rear porch steps in her bare feet, despite the fact that there was snow on the ground, to retrieve some blinds left out in the yard. (See Plaintiff's Deposition which has been filed with the court at page 34, 38). As she was re-entering the house, Plaintiff slipped on the porch steps and fell, injuring her elbow. (Plaintiff's Depo. at page 39).

Defendants Mark and Charlene Houser have filed a motion for summary judgment pursuant to Civ. R. 56(C).
II. LAW AND ARGUMENT
A. THE SUMMARY JUDGMENT STANDARD
Plaintiff has failed to carry her burden of setting forth specific facts and demonstrating genuine issues of material fact regarding each allegation of her complaint. See, Civ.R. 56(E).
A complete failure of proof concerning an essential element of the nonmoving party's case necessarily renders all other facts immaterial. As a result, a moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law where the nonmoving party failed to come forth with evidence of specific facts on an essential element of the case with respect to which he has the burden of proof. Black v. Cosentino (1996), 117 Ohio App.3d 40, 43 (citing Celotex Corp. v. Catrett (1986), 477 U.S. 317, 323).
In responding to a motion for summary judgment, the nonmoving party may not rest on bare allegations to demonstrate a factual dispute. Dresher v. Burt (1996), 75 Ohio St.3d 280, 293, 1996 Ohio 107, 662 N.E.2d 264. Additionally, a summary judgment motion must be overcome by specific and provable facts and not mere allegations; evidence of a possible inference is insufficient. Jackson v. Alert Fire and Safety Equip., Inc. (1991), 58 Ohio St.3d 48, 52; Cox v. Commercial Parts & Serv. (1994), 96 Ohio App.3d 417, 421. The key to the granting of summary judgment motion is that there are no genuine issues as to a material fact. Material facts are determined by substantive law. Only disputes over facts that might affect the outcome of a suit under governing law will properly preclude the grant of a motion for summary judgment. Irrelevant and unnecessary factual disputes will not be counted. Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242, 247-248; Perez v. Scripps-Howard Broadcasting (1988), 35 Ohio St.3d 215.

Here, plaintiff cannot set forth any evidence showing a material issue of fact for a jury to determine. Thus, defendants are entitled to summary judgment on each of plaintiff's claims.
B. NEGLIGENCE
To prevail in a negligence action, the plaintiff must prove the 1) the existence of a duty, 2) a breach of that duty, and 3) an injury proximately resulting from the breach of that duty. Menifee v. Ohio Welding Prods., Inc. (1984), 15 Ohio St.3d 75, 77, 472 N.E.2d 707. Plaintiff has failed to produce evidence that satisfies each of these three prongs.
1. Plaintiff was not a tenant at the time of the incident.
Plaintiff was not a party to the lease between Defendants and Mr. Morrison. (Exhibit A) . Defendants Mark and Charlene Houser initiated eviction proceedings against their tenant Patrick Morrison and Plaintiff on December 11, 2005. Mr. Houser posted the required three-day notice to leave the premises at the property, naming both Mr. Morrison and Plaintiff, as well as "all other occupants." (Exhibit C) Plaintiff's disingenuous affidavit to the contrary is insufficient to create a genuine question of material fact. By her own admission, Plaintiff did not pay any rent to the Housers. (Plaintiff's Depo. at page 13). Furthermore, the fact that Mr. Houser may at one time have considered Plaintiff to be a tenant has no impact on the legal relationship between the two parties at the time of the incident. Defendants owed no duty to the Plaintiff other than to refrain from willful, wanton or reckless conduct. Under Ohio law, a landlord owes the same duty to a guest of a tenant, lawfully on the premises, as he does to the tenant. (emphasis added) Shump v. First Continental-Robinwood Assocs. (1994), 71 Ohio St. 3d 414, 419, 644 N.E.2d 291, 294. As noted above, the Housers had initiated eviction proceedings against the tenant, Mr. Morrison, and all the other residents of 273 Cranz, including Plaintiff. Because plaintiff was not lawfully on the premises at the time of the incident, Shump is inapplicable.
3

.
Therefore, the Housers owed Plaintiff only the duty they owed to any other licensee "who enters the premises of another by permission or acquiescence, for his own pleasure or benefit." Light v. Ohio Univ. (1986), 28 Ohio St.3d 66, 68, 28 Ohio B. 165, 502 N.E.2d 611. That duty is merely to refrain from willful, wanton or reckless conduct that is likely to injure him. See Gladon v. Greater Cleveland Regional Transit Auth. (1996), 75 Ohio St.3d 312, 315, 1996 Ohio 137, 662 N.E.2d 287.
2. The Housers are not liable for Plaintiff's injuries, pursuant to R.C. 5321.04
The Ohio legislature created the Landlord-Tenant act to regulate residential property rental relationships. R.C. § 5321.04(A)(2) provides that a "landlord who is a party to a rental agreement shall ... (1) Comply with the requirements of all applicable building, housing, health, and safety codes that materially affect health and safety; (2) Make all repairs and do whatever is reasonably necessary to put and keep the premises in a fit and habitable condition."
A violation of a building code does not constitute negligence per se and is not conclusive proof of a party's negligence. Chambers v. St. Mary's School (1998), 82 Ohio St.3d 563, 568, 1998 Ohio 184, 697 N.E.2d 198. Rather, evidence of a code violation may be taken into consideration along with all other materials correctly submitted pursuant to Civ.R. 56(E) in order to determine whether a party was negligent. Id. An alleged violation of R.C. 5321.04 does not obviate a plaintiff's obligation to prove that the violation was the proximate cause of the injury complained of and that the landlord had notice of the defective condition. Shroades v. Rental Homes, Inc. (1981), 68 Ohio St. 2d 20, 25-26, 427 N.E.2d 774.1

While the issue of proximate cause is ordinarily a question of fact, in those situations where reasonable minds could not differ as to the matter of proximate cause because circumstances clearly indicate an obvious cause and effect relationship, the issue of proximate cause may be determined as a matter of law. See Zawkocki v. Houtz (1974), 40 Ohio App. 2d 118, 123, citing Ornella v. Robertson (1968), 14 Ohio St. 2d 144, 151. See, also, 70 Ohio Jurisprudence 3d (1986) 419, Negligence, Section 217.
Plaintiff cites the lack of a handrail on the back porch steps as the proximate cause of her injuries. During Plaintiff's deposition testimony she admitted that not only was she outside in the snow in her bare feet, she was carrying blinds that had been left out in the yard in her hands. (Plaintiff's Depo. at page 36). The blinds were, by her own admission "seven foot long." (Id.) Even if a handrail had been present, when Plaintiff slipped on the step it is unlikely that a handrail would have prevented her from falling, as her hands were not free to grab one. Therefore, the lack of a handrail was not the proximate cause of Plaintiff's injuries, and R.C. 5321.04 is inapplicable, under Shroades.
3. Plaintiff's common law negligence claim holds no merit
1
Without respect to Plaintiff's statutory claim, her common law claim must fail. (See Complaint, 15). Plaintiff claims that the steps she safely traversed no more than a minute or two before, suddenly became unreasonably dangerous when she walked back up the steps to the house. As the Supreme Court explained in Raflo v. Losantiville Country Club "one who upon entering a building traverses a step, the height of which is proscribed by the state building code, cannot maintain that the hazard was so insubstantial as to go unnoticed at that time, yet was unreasonably
'notice." (internal citations omitted.) Boyd at P22.

dangerous, hence actionable, when it occasioned her fall upon leaving the building." (1973), 34 Ohio St.2d 1, 295 N.E.2d 202, paragraph one of the syllabus. Similarly, "one who enters a building by traversing a step described as 'abnormally high,' is charged with knowledge of the presence of that abnormality upon exiting." Id., paragraph two of the syllabus, following Leighton v. Hower Corp. (1948), 149 Ohio St. 72, 77 N.E.2d 600.
When a danger is "open and obvious, a landowner owes no duty of care to individuals lawfully on the premises." Armstrong v. Best Buy Co., Inc., 99 Ohio St.3d 79, 2003-Onio-2573. In a factually similar case, the Ninth Appellate District held that the trial court properly granted summary judgment against the guest of a tenant who claimed that a defective porch handrail caused him to fall. Virde v. Stalnaker, 2004 Ohio 2671, P16 (Ohio Ct. App. 2004). Citing Raflo, the court held that his status on the property was governed by common law distinctions and that as an invitee, he traversed the known defect "at his peril." Id.
Plaintiff alleges that the lack of a handrail on the back porch steps was the cause of her injuries. She was aware of the lack of handrail when she safely went down the steps in her bare feet, out into the snow. She is charged with notice of the lack of a handrail and cannot claim that the steps became unreasonably dangerous during the few minutes that elapsed between her going down and then returning.
4. Plaintiff's own negligence was the cause of her injuries
In Mowery v. McCracken (August 31, 1987), Hancock App. No. 5-85-33, the court discussed whether summary judgment was ever appropriate in comparative negligence cases. Citing Tatro v. Harp (Sept. 26, 1984), Lucas C.P. No. 83-2422, the court stated that:
As a general rule, summary judgment should not be used in negligence actions, particularly under comparative negligence statutes which contemplate a weighing or balancing of the negligence of each party and a determination of the percentage of negligence attributable to

However, this is not to say that summary judgment is never appropriate; in rare cases it is permissable for a court to rule as a matter of law that one party's negligence exceeds that of the other. It is appropriate where the evidence of plaintiff's negligence is clear and the quantum so great, * * * and where the evidence is so conclusive that reasonable minds can come to only one conclusion.
To hold that summary judgment is never appropriate in comparative negligence actions would be to force all such cases to trial even in plain and indisputable cases, defeating the purpose of the summary judgment procedure which is to terminate expensive and needless litigation where no genuine issue of fact exists. It is this Court's opinion that such a result was surely not intended by the drafters of the comparative negligence statutes.
(Internal citations omitted) Id. at 10-11.
Ohio law recognizes contributory negligence as "any want of ordinary care on the part of the person injured, which combined and concurred with the defendant's negligence and contributed to the injury as a proximate cause thereof, and as an element without which the injury would not have occurred." Stiver v. Miami Valley Cable Council (1995), 663 N.E.2d 1310, quoting Brinkmoeller v. Wilson (1975), 41 Ohio St.2d 223, 226, 325 N.E.2d 233.
Plaintiff walked, in her bare feet, through the snow to get the blinds before she returned to the house with wet feet. (Plaintiff's Depo. at page 38). She was able to safely traverse the steps on the way down. The only difference between then and when she walked back up them was that her bare feet were wet from the snow and her hands were full. Her own negligence is solely responsible for her injuries.
5. Defendants Mark and Charlene Houser were not in exclusive possession and control over the area where the Plaintiff fell.
The evidence in this case is undisputed that the tenant, Patrick Morrison and the Plaintiff had exclusive possession and control of the leased property, and, further, were responsible for rehabilitating and maintaining the steps where plaintiff fell. Mark Houser stated in his deposition

that "Mr. Morrison, being a rehab guy, was going to perform some of the needed work on the house." (See Defendant Mark Houser's Deposition which has been filed with the court at page 9). In fact, Mr. Houser specifically directed Mr. Morrison to fix the things that were on the list of repairs required by the Health Department. (Houser Dep. at page 10). "It has been the rule in Ohio that a landlord out-of-possession is not liable to persons injured by reasons of the acts or failures of the tenant." Forester v. F.L.M., Inc. (1978), 60 Ohio App.2d 342. The lessor who does not retain the right to admit or exclude others from the premises has generally not reserved the degree of possession or control necessary to impose liability for the condition of the premises. Pitts v. Housing Authority (1953), 160 Ohio St. 129, 113 N.E.2d 869 ; Cooper v. Roose (1949), 151 Ohio St. 316, 85 N.E.2d 545. The testimony of defendant Mark Houser clearly establishes that Morrison had taken the responsibility to maintain the property and do necessary repairs. Accordingly, summary judgment is also appropriate on this ground.
However, even if the court finds that the Housers were in possession or control of the property, they are not liable for Plaintiff's injuries.
In Shump, the plaintiff decedent had been a social guest of the tenant, who succumbed to smoke inhalation allegedly due to the landlord's failure to properly install a smoke detector in the apartment, in violation of a city ordinance. 71 Ohio St. 3d at 415. The Ohio Supreme Court held in that case"the common-law classifications of trespasser, licensee, and invitee determine the legal duty that a tenant owes others who enter upon rental property that is in the exclusive control of the tenant. However, with regard to areas within the exclusive possession of a tenant, the common-law classifications do not affect the legal duty that a landlord owes a tenant or others lawfully upon the leased premises." (emphasis added), Id. at 417. Unless the court finds that Plaintiff was in control of the area where she fell, Shump is inapplicable and the Housers owe only a common law duty to

refrain from wanton or willful conduct.
Additionally, the Ninth Appellate District has declined to extend the Shump holding to cases involving injuries suffered from a mishap occurring in a common area. See, e.g. Sanders v. Bellevue Manor Apts.(Jan. 3, 1996), Lorain App. No. 95CA006067; Rios v. Shauck (June 3, 1998), Lorain App. No. 97CA006753. In those cases, the court held that as to common areas, the common law duty of care toward a licensee still applies, namely that the landlord will refrain from wanton and willful misconduct. While the property in question is a single-family unit, the outside entrance, walkway, and steps would generally be considered a common area in a multi-unit facility. As a matter of policy, there is no incentive to treat the two differently and this Court should accordingly grant summary judgment in favor of the Housers.
III. CONCLUSION
Defendants Mark and Charlene Houser submit that there are no genuine issues as to any material fact with respect to plaintiff's complaint, and that defendants are entitled to judgment as a matter of law for the following reasons:
1. Defendants owed Plaintiff, who was a licensee only the duty to refrain from wanton, willful or reckless conduct;
2. Plaintiff has failed to demonstrate the existence of an unsafe condition;
3. Plaintiff's own negligence was the cause of her injuries; and
4. Defendants were not in exclusive possession or control of the area where Plaintiff fell.
WHEREFORE, defendants, Mark and Charlene Houser, respectfully move this Court for an order granting summary judgment in favor of defendants as to plaintiff's complaint.

This cause was heard upon the record in the trial court. Each error assigned has been reviewed and the following disposition is made:
BAIRD, Judge.
[*P1] Appellant, David Virde, appeals a grant of summary judgment to William Stalnaker entered by the Summit County Court of Common Pleas. We reverse and remand.
1.
[*P2] On August 29, 2002, Virde filed a complaint
with the Summit County Court of Common Pleas naming Stalnaker as the defendant. In the complaint, Virde alleges the following: Virde stated that his wife, Karen and her friend, Michelle Dillar, entered into a lease agreement with Stalnaker, and at the time of the lease agreement, Virde was staying at Edwin Shaw Rehabilitation Hospital "following the amputation of [ ** 2] his right foot and leg, approximately eight inches below the knee." Shortly after the lease was signed, Virde moved into the premises with his wife and Dillar, "with the consent of" Stalnaker, and Stalnaker "knew, or should have known, that the handrail at the back steps to the premises was in serious disrepair[.]" The complaint further alleges that "the tenants asked Stalnaker to fix and repair the guardrail, but he failed and refused to do so." Virde claims that while he "was carefully coming down the stairs into the backyard" the handrail loosened and he "fell and seriously injured himself." Virde states that his injuries and losses resulted from Stalnaker's negligent failure to properly maintain or repair the handrail, Stalnaker created a nuisance or dangerous condition knowing that Virde would likely be injured, and Stalnaker failed to warn. nl Lastly, Virde alleged that Stalnaker's failure to repair the railing violated R.C. 5321.04 and is, therefore, negligence per se.
nl The complaint also contains allegations of housing discrimination, retaliatory eviction, and interference with fair housing rights. The trial court found for Stalnaker on these counts; however, the trial court's disposition of these counts is not part of this appeal.

[*P3] On July 7, 2003, Stalnaker filed notice of filing the following deposition transcripts; the depositions of David Virde, taken on May 10 and 14, 2003; that of Michelle Dillar, taken on October 18, 2001; and, that of Karen Virde Johnson, taken on May 17, 2003. IT.
Assignment of Error
"THE TRIAL COURT ERRED IN GRANTING STALNAKER'S MOTION FOR SUMMARY JUDGMENT AS THE RECORD SHOWS THERE WERE GENUINE ISSUES OF MATERIAL FACT IN DISPUTE AND THAT STALNAKER WAS NOT ENTITLED TO JUDGMENT AS A MATTER OF LAW."
[*P5] Virde argues that the trial court's ruling that Virde was a trespasser on Stalnaker's property is "utterly unwarranted [ ** 4] and is clearly contradicted by the evidence" because Virde was an authorized guest of the tenants, "was lawfully on the premises," and Stalnaker was aware he lived there. Moreover, Virde claims that there was a genuine issue of material fact, as evidence by the deposition testimony, regarding Virde's actual status as a trespasser, a licensee, or an invitee. Virde then argues that "the evidence clearly established Virde was an invitee." Additionally, Virde claims, as an invitee, Stalnaker owed him a duty and "the fact that Virde knew the railing was 'loose' does not mean he was aware it would give way or that Stalnaker was absolved of all liability for anything that thereafter happened[.]" Lastly Virde urges that Stalnaker's failure to repair is negligence per se because Stalnaker violated Sec. 5321.04 of the Landlords and Tenants Act of 1974.
[*P6] We begin by noting that an appellate court
reviews an award of summary judgment de novo. Grafton v. Ohio Edison Co. (1996), 77 Ohio St. 3d 102, 105, 1996 Ohio 336, 671 N.E.2d 241. We apply the same standard as the trial court, viewing the facts in the case in the light most favorable to the non-moving party and resolving any doubt in favor of [ ** 5] the non-moving party. Viock v. Stowe-Woodward Co. (1983), 13 Ohio App. 3d 7. 12, 13 Ohio B. 8, 467 N.E.2d 1378.
[*P7] Pursuant to Civil Rule 56(C), summary judgment is proper if:
"(1) No genuine issue as to any material fact remains to be litigated; (2) the moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law; and (3) it appears from the evidence that reasonable minds can come to but one conclusion, and viewing such evidence most strongly in favor of the party against whom the motion for summary judgment is made, that conclusion is adverse to that party." Temple v. Wean United, Inc. (1977), 50 Ohio St. 2d 317, 327, 364 N.E.2d 267.
[*P8] To prevail on a motion for summary judgment, the party moving for summary judgment bears the initial burden of informing the trial court of the basis for the motion and pointing to parts of the record that show the absence of a genuine issue of material fact. Dresher v. Burt (1996), 75 Ohio St. 3d 280, 293-294, 1996 Ohio 107, 662 N.E.2d 264. Where the non-moving party would have the burden of proving a number of elements in order to prevail at trial, the party moving for summary judgment may point to evidence that the non-moving party cannot possibly prevail on [ ** 6] an essential element of the claim. See, e.g., Stivison v. Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co. (1997), 80 Ohio St. 3d 498, 499, 1997 Ohio 321, 687 N.E.2d 458. In that case, the moving party then "bears the initial burden of demonstrating that there are no genuine issues of material fact concerning an essential element of the opponent's case." Dresher, 75 Ohio St. 3d at 292. The burden would then shift to the non-moving party to show that there is a genuine issue of material fact as to that element. Id. at 293.
[*P9] The Ohio Supreme Court has explained the summary judgment burden as follows:
"The movant must be able to point to evidentiary materials of the type listed in Civ.R. 56(C) that a court is to consider in rendering summary judgment. The evidentiary materials listed in Civ.R. 56(C) include 'the

pleadings, depositions, answers to interrogatories, written admissions, affidavits, transcripts of evidence in the pending case, and written stipulations of fact, if any.' These evidentiary materials must show that there is no genuine issue as to any material fact, and that the moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law. While the movant is not necessarily obligated [ ** 7] to place any of these evidentiary materials in the record, the evidence must be in the record or the motion cannot succeed." Id. at 292-293.
[*P10] Only after the movant satisfies the initial Dresher burden, must the nonmoving party then present evidence that some issue of material fact remains for the trial court to resolve. Id. at 294. "It is basic that regardless of who may have the burden of proof at trial, the burden is on the party moving for summary judgment to establish that there is no genuine issue of material fact and that the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law." Horizon Savings v. Wootton (1991), 73 Ohio App. 3d 501, 504, 597 N.E.2d 1150.
[*P11] In order to prevail on his claim, Virde was required to prove that the defendant owed a duty of care to him, that the defendant breached that duty, and that the breach of the duty proximately caused his injury. Chambers v. St. Mary's School (1998), 82 Ohio St. 3d 563, 565, 1998 Ohio 184, 697 N.E.2d 198. However, assuming that Stalnaker had met his burden, Virde could defeat summary judgment by showing that there were still genuine issues of material fact to be resolved. See Dresher, 75 Ohio St. 3d at 292-293. [ ** 8]
[*P12] We first address the allegation of negligence per se. In his complaint, Virde alleges that Stalnaker's failure to repair the railing is negligence per se because Stalnaker violated a duty to repair codified at R.C. 5321.04:
"(A) A landlord who is a party to a rental agreement shall do all of the following:
****
"(2) Make all repairs and do whatever is reasonably necessary to put and keep the premises in a fit and habitable condition[.]"
[*P13] "In landowner liability cases, the duty of care owed depends upon the status of the plaintiff, as 'Ohio adheres to the common-law classifications of
invitee, licensee, and trespasser." Qualchoice, Inc. v. Yost Constr. Co., Inc. (Jan. 5, 2000), 9th Dist. No. 98CA007224, 2000 Ohio App. LEXIS 8, at 10, quoting Gladon v. Greater Cleveland Regional Transit Auth. (1996), 75 Ohio St. 3d 312, 315, 1996 Ohio 137, 662 N.E.2d 287. However, a duty imposed by statute is an exception to the common law; R.C. 5321.04 clearly imposes upon landlords a duty to repair. Schoefield v. Beulah Road, Inc. (Aug. 26, 1999), 10th Dist. No 98AP-1475, 1999 Ohio App. LEXIS 3926, citing Shroades v. Rental Homes (1981), 68 Ohio St. 2d 20, 427 N.E.2d 774. [ ** 9] "A violation of a statute that sets forth specific duties constitutes negligence per se." Schoefield, supra. A landowner owes the same duties to persons lawfully upon the leased premises as the landlord owes to the tenant. Shump v. First Continental-Robinwood Assoc. (1994), 71 Ohio St. 3d 414, 420, 1994 Ohio 427, 644 N.E.2d 291.
[*P14] In addressing the count of negligence per se, Stalnaker states in the motion for summary judgment only that the doctrine doesn't apply to Virde because Virde was not a tenant and the statute applies only to a tenant. Virde argues in reply that the holding of Schump required the trial court to extend the negligence per se doctrine to him. We agree that Shump controls. A landlord is liable under Shump if: (1) the plaintiff was within the class of persons intended to be protected by the statute; (2) the harm suffered was the type of harm against which the statute was intended to guard; (3) the plaintiff establishes proximate cause; and (4) the plaintiff show that the landlord received notice of the defective condition of the rental premises, that the landlord knew of the defect, or that the tenant had made reasonable, but unsuccessful, attempts [ ** 10] to notify the landlord. Primes v. Milbry (Nov. 19, 1997), 9th Dist. No 18236, 1997 Ohio App. LEXIS 5180, at 4. Stalnaker, in order to meet his burden under Civ.R. 56, must demonstrate, through the evidence, that he had no notice of the defective condition of the rental premises and that he did not know of the defect. See 1997 Ohio App. LEXIS 5180, at 6-7. Stalnaker submitted deposition testimony from Dillar wherein she stated that the house was well maintained and she did not report to Stalnaker that repairs were required. Likewise Karen Virde stated in her deposition that she did not contact Stalnaker about the loose rail; however,
"It was either [Dillar or Virde] that either told him or called the office. *** But I do know that somebody was

In Virde's deposition, he was asked if "during the time that you stayed there, did you request that Mr. Stalnaker do any type of repair work to the property?" He was also asked, "So you never at any time talked to [Stalnaker] or any of his staff about doing anything at that unit?" Virde answered in the negative to both questions. We must resolve two issues in order to decide this appeal: (1) under what circumstances may summary judgment be granted in a case governed by the [*5] comparative negligence provisions of R.C. 2315.19; and (2) whether those circumstances are present in the case before us. Based upon our analysis of these issues, it is appropriate to address all three assignments of error together.
(1)
In Harless v. Willis Day Warehousing Co. (1978), 54 Ohio St. 2d 64, the Supreme Court of Ohio held:
"The appositeness of rendering a summary judgment hinges upon the tripartite demonstration: (1) that there is no genuine issue as to any material fact; (2) that the moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law; and (3) that reasonable minds can come to but one conclusion, and that conclusion is adverse to the party against whom the motion for summary judgment is made, who is entitled to have the evidence construed most strongly in his favor." Id. at 66.
In requesting summary judgment, the moving party has the burden of proving that no geniune issue of fact remains for trial. Id. However, once the moving party has met its burden, the opposing party must take affirmative action to defeat the motion by showing a genuine issue for trial. Benjamin v. Deffet Rentals (1981), 66 Ohio St. 2d 86.
To defeat a motion for [*6] summary judgment filed by a defendant in a negligence action it has been held that the plaintiff must "* * * identify a duty, or duties, owed him by the defendant, and the evidence must be sufficient, considered most favorably to the plaintiff, to allow reasonable minds to infer that a specific duty was breached, that the breach of duty was the proximate cause of plaintiff's injury, and that plaintiff was injured." Patete v. Benko (1986), 29 Ohio App. 3d 325, 327, quoting Keister v. Park Centre Lanes (1981), 3 Ohio App. 3d 19, syllabus, and citing also Wellman v. East Ohio Gas Co. (1953), 160 Ohio St. 103.
In Burgard v. Eff (1965), 1 Ohio App. 2d 483, the Court of Appeals for Lucas County held that a common pleas court may not enter summary judgment on behalf of defendants in a negligence case ** * * unless it could determine from the documents *** [which it may consider on] the hearing of such motion, as a matter of

In a decision which might be construed as only slightly updating the criteria of Burgard v. Eff, supra, to accommodate the comparative negligence provisions of R.C. 2315.19, enacted in 1980, the Court of Appeals for Cuyahoga County has held that summary judgment may be granted to defendants in a negligence suit where, after construing the undisputed evidence most strongly in favor of plaintiff, a reasonable person could only conclude that the contributory negligence of the plaintiff was greater than the combined negligence of the defendants. Mitchell v. Ross (1984), 14 Ohio App. 3d 75, 78. Moreover, it is clear that in making such a determination, conduct previously considered as assumption of the risk by the plaintiff, while no longer a complete defense, remains viable nevertheless as a "species" of the plaintiff's contributory negligence to be weighed against the alleged negligence of the defendant pursuant to R.C. 2315.19. Mitchell v. Ross, supra, at 77; Anderson v. Ceccardi (1983), 6 Ohio St. 3d 110, 113.
In view of the foregoing authority, [*8] we therefore hold that summary judgment is properly granted in favor of the defendant in a comparative negligence case where, pursuant to the criteria of Civ. R. 56(C), the court can make any one of the following determinations as a matter of law: either, (1) the defendant was not negligent; or (2) the defendant's negligence, if any, was not the proximate cause of plaintiff's injury (such as where the plaintiff's own negligence was the sole proximate cause of the injury) or (3) the plaintiff's own negligence, (considering factors of assumption of the risk, if any,) outweighed any negligence of the defendant under R.C. 2315.19.

A.
Plaintiff's first assignment of error is that the trial court applied an incorrect standard to determine what duty defendant owed her. In support of its motion for summary judgment in the trial court, defendant argued that plaintiff was a licensee on defendant's property at the time of her fall and that, accordingly, the extent of its duty was to refrain from engaging in willful or wanton conduct to her detriment. In her response to defendant's motion for summary judgment, plaintiff did not dispute her status as a licensee, but rather argued that defendant had engaged in willful or wanton conduct toward her:
"When all facts and inferences are considered, there are genuine issues of fact regarding whether Defendant's conduct was wanton or willful and whether it had, under the circumstances, intent to injure or design to injure the Plaintiff." Plaintiff's Brief in Opposition [*5] to Motion for Summary Judgment at 6.
Following submission of plaintiff's response to defendant's motion for summary judgment to the trial court, but before the trial court ruled on defendant's motion, the Ohio Supreme Court decided Shump v. First Continental-Robinwood (1994), 71 Ohio St. 3d 414, 644 N.E.2d 291, in which it held that "[a] landlord owes the same duties to persons lawfully upon the leased premises as the landlord owes to the tenant." Id. at syllabus. In granting defendant's motion for summary judgment, the trial court specifically held that defendant "did not commit any act of willful or wanton misconduct." Plaintiff has argued to this Court that, in view of the Supreme Court's decision in Shump, defendant owed plaintiff a duty of ordinary care rather than the lesser duty of refraining from willful or wanton misconduct.
Shump was an action by the administrator of the estate of a woman who had died from fumes of a fire in an apartment in which she was an overnight guest. The administrator alleged that the decedent's death was proximately caused by the landlord's failure to install a smoke detector on the first floor of the apartment in violation of [*6] a city ordinance. The landlord argued that the decedent was an invitee in the apartment and that its only duty to her was to refrain from willful or wanton misconduct. The Ohio Supreme Court determined, however, that the landlord owed the decedent the same duty that it owed the tenant of the apartment in which she died:
The common-law classifications of trespasser, licensee, and invitee determine the legal duty that a tenant owes others who enter upon rental property that is in the exclusive control of the tenant. However, with regard to areas within the exclusive possession of a tenant, the common-law classifications do not affect the legal duty that a landlord owes a tenant or others lawfully upon the leased premises. * * * In the case at hand, it is undisputed that the apartment was in the exclusive possession of [the tenant] when

Id. at 417 (emphasis in original).
Plaintiff in this case was not injured on premises that were in the exclusive control of a tenant. Rather, she was injured in a parking lot that was in the landlord's control. The Supreme Court's decision in Shump had [*7] no impact on the duty owed plaintiff in this case. Further, as discussed below, even if, as contended by plaintiff, defendant owed her a duty of ordinary care, the undisputed evidence in this case established no breach of that duty. Plaintiff's first assignment of error is overruled.
B.
Plaintiff's second assignment of error is that defendant was not entitled to judgment as a matter of law. As discussed above, plaintiff was a licensee on defendant's property at the time of her injury. Plaintiff, however, has argued that, in view of the Supreme Court's decision in Shump, defendant owed her a duty of ordinary care. For purposes of this assignment of error, this Court will assume that defendant owed plaintiff a duty of ordinary care. Generally, an owner of a business owes its customers a duty of ordinary care in maintaining the premises in a reasonably safe condition so that those customers are neither unnecessarily nor unreasonably exposed to danger. Paschal v. Rite Aid Pharmacy Inc. (1985), 18 Ohio St. 3d 203, 480 N.E.2d 474. As this Court recently noted in Davis v. Friendly's Ice Cream Corporation (September 27, 1995), Summit App. No. 17094, unreported, the duty of ordinary [*8] care, however, does not make a business owner an insurer of its customers' safety. "It also does not require the owner to protect invitees from dangers which are known to the invitee or are so obvious and apparent that the invitee may reasonably be expected to discover them and protect himself." Id. at 3, citing Paschal v. Rite Aid Pharmacy Inc. (1985), 18 Ohio St. 3d 203, 203-204, 480 N.E.2d 474.
Plaintiff has complained about two things regarding the parking lot where she fell. First she has complained about the concrete wheel stops. She testified at her deposition, however, that she had been aware of the presence of those wheel stops from her prior visits to her daughter:
Q. You knew that there were these
concrete stops present in this parking area, didn't you?
A. No, I never -- I never even thought about that.
Q. But you had seen them before, had you not?
A. Well, the daytime.
Q. So you were aware from your prior visits during the daytime that these concrete stops were present along the front of the apartment complex?
A. Well, I knew they were there, but, I mean, not at night, you know.
Plaintiff also indicated that she was aware [*9] that the concrete stops were not fastened down and sometimes would be pushed out of place. There was no evidence, however, that the stop over which she tripped was out of place at the time of her fall.
Even assuming defendant owed plaintiff a duty of ordinary care, that duty did not include an obligation to warn her of the presence of the concrete wheel stops because she already knew about them. Defendant, therefore, did not breach any duty to plaintiff regarding the concrete wheel stops.

C.
Plaintiff's third assignment of error is that the determination of whether defendant acted willfully or wantonly was a question of fact for the jury. Once a party has moved for summary judgment and has argued that the opposing party will not be able to submit evidence sufficient to carry her burden on an issue for which the opposing party will have the burden of proof at trial, in order to avoid entry of summary judgment against it, the party opposing summary judgment must submit evidence, or point to evidence already in the record, that would be sufficient to carry her burden of proof at trial:
There is no issue for trial
unless there is sufficient evidence favoring the nonmoving party for a jury to return a verdict for that party. * * * If the evidence
is merely colorable, * *
* or is not significantly probative, * * * summary judgment may be granted.
Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc. (1986), 477 U.S. 242, 249-250, 91 L. Ed. 2d 202, 212, 106 S. Ct. 2505.
As discussed in regard to plaintiff's second assignment [*11] of error, the evidence in the record would not have been sufficient to permit a jury to return a verdict in plaintiff's favor, even assuming that defendant owed her a duty of ordinary care. Accordingly, that evidence also would not have been sufficient to permit a jury to conclude that defendant had engaged in willful or wanton conduct that proximately caused plaintiff's injuries. Plaintiff's third assignment of error is overruled.
III.
Plaintiff's assignments of error are overruled. The judgment of the trial court is affirmed.
Judgment affirmed.

This cause was heard upon the record in the trial court. Each error assigned has been reviewed and the following disposition is made:
DICKINSON, Judge.
Plaintiff Luis A. Rios has appealed from an order of the Lorain County Common Pleas Court that granted summary judgment to defendants Robert and Barbara Shauck. He has argued that the trial court incorrectly applied the "two-inch rule" to find that a defect on an
interior staircase landing on rental property was not unreasonably unsafe as a matter of law. This Court affirms the judgment of the trial court because the defect on the staircase landing was open and obvious in that plaintiff had actual knowledge of its existence.
I.
On December 31, 1994, plaintiff tripped on a bulge in a carpet that covered a staircase [*2] landing on defendants' property, fracturing his foot. At the time, plaintiff was living with a tenant who rented one of four units at that residential property. Apparently, another tenant had dropped a refrigerator on the landing, making a hole. That tenant covered the hole with a board, then placed the carpet over the entire area. The board was approximately 3/4" thick and raised the carpet by at least that height.
On July 12, 1996, plaintiff filed a complaint against defendants in the Lorain County Common Pleas Court. On February 14, 1997, defendants moved for summary judgment. Plaintiff responded, and, on March 25, 1997, the trial court granted summary judgment to defendants. Specifically, the trial court determined that plaintiff had actual knowledge of the condition. Furthermore, it determined that the carpet bulge was about one inch and that there were no attendant circumstances that made the bulge unreasonably unsafe. Consequently, defendants were not responsible for plaintiff's injuries. Plaintiff timely appealed to this Court.
IT.
Plaintiff's assignment of error is that the trial court incorrectly applied the two-inch rule to an interior defect

in a common staircase [*3] landing of a residential rental premises. Both plaintiff and defendants have confined their briefs to discussions of the "two-inch rule." That rule, as developed by the Ohio Supreme Court, is that a difference in elevation in a sidewalk or walkway of less than two inches is considered insubstantial as a matter of law and, therefore, does not present a question for a jury, unless attendant circumstances exist that render the defect substantial. See, e.g., Kimball v. Cincinnati (1953), 160 Ohio St. 370, 116 N.E.2d 708, Cash v. Cincinnati (1981), 66 Ohio St. 2d 319, 421 N.E.2d 1275, and Stockhauser v. Archdiocese of Cincinnati (1994), 97 Ohio App. 3d 29, 33, 646 N.E.2d 198. Plaintiff has argued that the two-inch rule "evolved in the context of exterior conditions" and should not have been applied to this case, when his injuries were caused by an interior defect on rental property. This Court, however, need not decide the applicability of the two-inch rule to this case.
Plaintiff has premised his argument on a theory that, as a social guest of a tenant, he was entitled to the protections of the Ohio Landlord-Tenant Act, particularly Section 5321.04 of the Ohio Revised Code. [*4] See Shump v. First Continental-Robinwood Assoc. (1994), 71 Ohio St. 3d 414, 644 N.E.2d 291, syllabus. Plaintiff, however, was injured in a common area, namely, the staircase landing leading to the upstairs apartments. This Court, in distinguishing Shump, has held that a social guest, injured in an area not in the exclusive control of the tenant, is owed a duty of care by the landlord no higher than that owed to a licensee. See Sanders v. Bellevue Manor Apts. (Jan. 3, 1996), Lorain App. No. 95CA006067, unreported, 1996 Ohio App. LEXIS 3, at *6-7. But see McCool v. Hillbrook Apts. (Aug. 23, 1995), Mahoning App. No. 93CA200, unreported, 1995 Ohio App. LEXIS 3538, at *4-5 (holding that a social guest of a tenant is an invitee). Consequently, plaintiff, as a social guest of the woman with whom he was living, was not protected by Section 5321.04 of the Ohio Revised Code while on the staircase landing, and the decision in Shump had no impact on the duty of care owed plaintiff. See Sanders, 1996 Ohio App. LEXIS 3, at *6-7.
Instead, defendants owed plaintiff only the common law duty of care applicable to licensees or, at most, the duty owed to invitees. The duty owed [*5] to a licensee is to refrain from wantonly or wilfully causing injury, while the duty owed to an invitee is one of ordinary care. See Provencher v. Ohio Dept. of Transp. (1990), 49 Ohio St. 3d 265, 266, 551 N.E.2d 1257. In this case, whether
plaintiff was a licensee or an invitee, defendants did not breach the duty of care that they owed him. A landlord owes no duty to warn a tenant's social guest of known dangers in common areas. See Sanders, 1996 Ohio App. LEXIS 3, at * 7-8; Stoner v. Wendy's Old-Fashioned Hamburgers (Apr. 20, 1994), Summit App. No. 16316, unreported, 1994 Ohio App. LEXIS 1744, at * 3-4.
In his deposition, plaintiff admitted that he knew about the hole in the floor and the board placed over the hole, which caused the carpet to bulge:
Q. Okay. Was this the first time that you had noticed that there was something underneath that carpet?
A. No.
Q. When had you noticed it before?
A. Well, the neighbor upstairs *** we had talked about it before, because it was, you could as soon as you would step on it, you would feel how the board was, you know, that there was something there.
Q. Okay.
A. And I guess, you know, that we all knew it was there.
Q. [*6] Okay. So before this incident happened you knew that there was something that you would step on that was a difference in height?
A. Yes, yes.
Plaintiff knew that the carpet on the staircase landing was uneven. In the face of such knowledge, he continued to use the staircase, apparently without any caution on his part to descend slowly or to watch his footing as he walked. Consequently, defendants were not liable for his injuries. Plaintiff's assignment of error is overruled.
III.
Plaintiff's assignment of error is overruled. The judgment of the trial court is affirmed.
Judgment affirmed.
